The Bahamian hutia (Geocapromys ingrahami) is a medium-sized hystricomorph rodent endemic to the Bahamas, exhibiting life-history traits characteristic of an island mammal with delayed development and low reproductive output. Under controlled captive conditions maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and available reproductive data indicate that they are capable of producing approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year]. This exceptionally low annual reproductive rate, reflecting the maximum reproductive output of the species, is consistent with a K-selected strategy typical of insular rodents with limited predation pressure and stable resource availability. Neonates, which are born in an advanced state of development relative to many other rodent taxa, have a wet weight at birth of 80 grams [Wwb = 80 grams], a relatively substantial mass that likely facilitates rapid postnatal growth and early mobility. The species appears to invest heavily in each offspring from the moment of parturition.

The developmental trajectory following parturition is marked by a relatively prolonged period of maternal dependence before nutritional independence is achieved. At a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 53 days [tx = 53 days], a duration that reflects the extended lactation period typical of hystricognath rodents. By the time the weaning process is complete, suckling juveniles attain a wet weight at weaning of 250 grams [Wwx = 250 grams], representing a more than threefold increase over their birth mass and signaling substantial somatic investment during the nursing stage. This weight gain is supported by the high lipid content of hutia milk, which is characteristic of mammals that produce relatively slow-growing, precocial young. The dietary transition from exclusive milk ingestion to solid food consumption is typically gradual, beginning several weeks before complete nutritional emancipation.

Reproductive maturation in the Bahamian hutia occurs considerably later than in most comparably sized rodents, a pattern consistent with its slow life-history strategy. Under the same thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females is 730 days [tp = 730 days], meaning that most females do not become reproductively active until their second year of life. This protracted delay before the onset of gonad maturation likely reflects the energetic requirements of achieving a sufficiently large body size for successful reproduction. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults, 660 grams [Wwi = 660 grams], provides a context for understanding this delayed maturation: females must more than double their weaning mass before they can sustain the metabolic demands of gestation and lactation. This pattern stands in contrast to smaller, more fecund rodents, which often become sexually mature within a few months.

Gestation in Geocapromys ingrahami is notably extended for a rodent of its body size, consistent with the general trend among hystricomorphs towards lengthy pregnancy. At a maintained temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the gestation time is 117 days [tg = 117 days], a period akin to that observed in medium-sized ungulates and considerably longer than the typical 21- to 30-day gestation of murid rodents. This prolonged uterine development allows for the delivery of a single, well-developed pup capable of thermoregulation and coordinated locomotion shortly after birth. The combination of a single offspring per pregnancy, a lengthy gestation, and an extended lactation period contributes to the species' very low annual recruitment potential, which is likely buffered in its natural habitat by low adult mortality.

Longevity data from captive colonies indicate that the Bahamian hutia has a remarkably long lifespan given its body mass, further emphasizing its position at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. When maintained under favorable captive conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan approaches 6.3 years [am = 6.3 years], with some individuals surviving considerably longer under optimal husbandry. This exceptional longevity, nearly five times the predicted lifespan for a rodent of this asymptotic mass (660 grams) [Wwi = 660 grams] based on allometric scaling relationships, is consistent with the species' low metabolic rate and the reduced extrinsic mortality pressures typical of isolated island ecosystems. The asymptotic body mass of 660 grams [Wwi = 660 grams] itself represents a moderate size for a hystricomorph, and the combination of delayed sexual maturation at around two years after birth (730 days since birth) [tp = 730 days since birth] with a long reproductive window allows for multiple breeding opportunities across an individual's lifetime, partially compensating for the very low annual output of a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] delivered approximately once each year [F_R_i = approximately once each year] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].
